slides.say: Nagarjuna's Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way. Chapter twenty-six: the examination of the twelve links.

slides.heading: Why does suffering keep coming back?
points: We get what we wanted, and want something else
We lose what we loved, and grieve
The Buddha's answer: a chain of twelve links
slides.say: Why does suffering keep coming back? We get what we wanted and want something else. We lose what we loved and grieve. One life, the tradition says, leads to another in the same way. The Buddha's answer was a chain of twelve links: from confusion to action, from action to a new life, from contact to feeling, from feeling to craving, and from craving to birth, ageing and death. This chapter sets out that chain.

slides.heading: A chapter with no refutation
points: After twenty-five chapters, how things work
Emptiness is why the world can work
Suffering made when ignorance is present, ended when it ends
slides.say: It is the one chapter of the work with no refutation in it. After twenty-five chapters showing that nothing is found standing on its own, Nagarjuna explains how things work. That is the point. Emptiness does not stop the world working; it is why the world can work. Dependent arising, the subject of the homage in chapter one, is here shown doing its everyday job: producing suffering when ignorance is present, and ending it when ignorance ends.

slides.heading: The verses
points: A new translation from the Sanskrit
The Sanskrit is shown above each verse
slides.say: First, the verses. The translation is new, made from the Sanskrit for this site.

slides.heading: The twelve links
slides.say: Now the explanation. The twelve links are the Buddha's own map of how suffering keeps itself going. Ignorance: not seeing how things are, taking them to exist from their own side. Formations: actions of body, speech and mind shaped by that ignorance. Consciousness, which those actions carry into a new life. Name and form, the mind and body of that life. The six sense fields. Contact, where sense, object and consciousness meet. Feeling, pleasant, unpleasant or neither. Craving. Grasping. Becoming, the build-up toward a new existence. Birth. And ageing and death, with all their sorrow. Ignorance, craving and grasping, filled in the diagram, keep the wheel turning. The links are often read over three lives, but the same chain can be seen in a single afternoon: confusion shapes an action, something is seen, a feeling comes, craving follows, and the grip of I must have this gives birth to a new little world of worry, which grows old and dies. Both readings are traditional.

slides.heading: From ignorance to a new life
points: Formations cut a riverbed for the next life
Consciousness 'enters': nothing passes over
Name-and-form, and the six sense fields
slides.say: The chain starts with ignorance. Covered over by it, a person makes formations in three ways, through body, speech and mind. These are not just deeds done and gone. They shape a direction, the way a river cuts its bed, and the next life flows along that bed. Consciousness, conditioned by formations, enters the new destiny. This sounds like a traveller moving house. It is not meant that way. Nothing passes over; the old flame lights a new one, as Nagasena said of rebirth. Once consciousness has entered, name and form, the mind and body of the new life, takes shape, and with it the six sense fields.

slides.heading: How experience is built
slides.say: Verses four and five slow down at the moment that matters most for practice: contact. Seeing does not happen inside a finished eye looking at a finished object. Visual consciousness arises in dependence on the eye, on visible form, and on attention. The verse sums these up as name and form: eye and visible form are the form side, attention the mental side. The meeting of eye, form and consciousness is called contact. From contact comes feeling. Then craving: we crave for the sake of feeling, more of the pleasant, an end to the unpleasant. Craving grows into grasping, at pleasures, at views, at rules and rituals, and at a self. With grasping, becoming arises. And verse seven adds its own escape clause: one who did not grasp would be freed, and there would be no becoming. The step from feeling to craving is where a practitioner can watch the chain at work.

slides.heading: This whole mass of suffering
points: Becoming, birth, ageing, death, sorrow and despair
'Whole' or 'only': nothing else in it
No one who owns the suffering, only the suffering
slides.say: Becoming is the five aggregates, the body and mind of a new life. From it comes birth, and from birth everything that follows: ageing, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress and despair. This whole mass of suffering is the Buddha's own phrase. It is called whole, or only, because there is nothing else in it. Chandrakirti reads the word as without a self or anything belonging to a self: no one who owns the suffering, only the suffering, arising from its conditions.

slides.heading: Who does it, and how it stops
slides.say: Verse ten gives the moral. The one who does not know is the maker of the formations, the root of samsara. The one who knows makes none, because they see how things are. This is not a change of fate imposed from outside. It is the plain consequence of the chain: the formations that lead to new suffering are made by not-knowing. Take away the not-knowing, and nothing is left to make them. So the chain can stop. When ignorance ceases, formations do not arise. And ignorance ceases through cultivating this very knowledge: for Chandrakirti, seeing dependent arising as it really is, which is seeing its emptiness. The chain does not have to be broken link by link. Remove the first condition, and the rest, losing their conditions in turn, do not arise. The whole mass of suffering comes to an end.

slides.heading: Why the chapter is here
points: Earlier: nothing arises from its own side
Here: how things arise as the world speaks
Empty links can work, and so can be ended
slides.say: A reader who has followed the earlier chapters may be surprised. Chapter one found no arising from self, other, both or neither. How can this chapter speak so plainly of one thing arising from another? The answer is the two truths. The earlier chapters asked whether things arise from their own side, and found that they do not. This chapter describes how they arise as the world speaks: in dependence, each link named in relation to the others. More than that, the working chain needs the emptiness found earlier. A chain whose links had natures of their own could never stop. Ignorance with its own nature could never be removed. Because the links are empty, the chain works, and because it works, it can be ended. Chandrakirti treats the chapter as the conventional account, fully endorsed, of how samsara runs.

slides.heading: What is left standing
points: Karma, rebirth, and the path that ends suffering
Left out: only the owner
The maker of samsara is not a person but not-knowing
slides.say: Everything the tradition relies on is kept here: karma, rebirth, the link between what we do and what we become, and the path that ends suffering. What is left out is only the owner. There is no self that travels through the twelve links, no I who ages and dies from its own side. Verse nine calls it a mass of suffering with nothing else in it, and verse ten makes the maker of samsara not a person but not-knowing.

slides.heading: Check it now
points: A pleasant feeling turns into wanting
An unpleasant one into pushing away
Seen as a meeting of conditions, the wheel need not turn
slides.say: The chain can be watched in any hour. Notice the next time a pleasant feeling turns into wanting, or an unpleasant one into pushing away. That step, from feeling to craving, is where the wheel turns. Seen clearly, as a meeting of conditions with no one behind it, it does not have to turn.

slides.heading: In the books
points: Substrateless World: Chapters 1, 8 and 9
Death and Continuity (bonus article)
Talks: Carrierless Continuity; Causal Efficacy
slides.say: The two books take up these themes in several places. In The Logical Necessity of a Substrateless World: chapter one, on innate grasping, the ignorance that heads the chain; chapter eight, on Nagasena's lamp and karmic continuity with nothing passing over; and chapter nine, on the mere I that acts and experiences the results of its actions. The bonus article Death and Continuity describes continuity like a candle through the night, without an invariant bearer. Two talks on YouTube take it up too: Carrierless Continuity, and Causal Efficacy Without Causal Power. Links to all of them are on the chapter page.
